Job averages can also miss differences between people doing nominally similar work. The appropriate reading is a qualified result for a specific exposure method and window, with human scientific review still pending.

modules.title: What the meningioma report contributes

overview.text: Low-frequency occupational fields differ from radiofrequency communication signals. ICNIRP’s overview distinguishes electric and magnetic components and explains induced electric fields and stimulation at sufficient levels. Work tasks can create intermittent and spatially uneven exposure, so a single averaged label may miss important features.

Our recovered primary outcome report concerns meningioma in Swedish case-control data. It assigned exposure from occupations rather than measuring each worker. That provides a defined epidemiological comparison, while leaving uncertainty about individual dose and other workplace outcomes. Scientific appraisal and reconciliation with related Swedish reports remain pending.

takeaway: The recovered meningioma analysis used a job-exposure matrix and found no overall association. Workplace field assessment still needs the actual equipment and work pattern.
title: Occupational low-frequency fields

faqs.a: No. It also uses switched gradients and RF components, each with a different exposure description.
faqs.q: Is MRI just exposure to a static magnet?

faqs.a: No. Patient medical exposure has a distinct scope and requires the clinical and MRI safety assessment relevant to that procedure.
faqs.q: Can a general environmental limit decide whether I should have a scan?

intro: An MRI system combines a strong static field with changing gradients and RF pulses. Patient procedures and staff movement need different assessments.

modules.label: Properties

paragraphs.text: A static magnetic field does not oscillate over time and is described by magnetic flux density in tesla. It has no oscillation wavelength to compare with radio waves. During MRI, other components vary with time, so a scanner’s nominal static field alone cannot describe RF energy deposition or gradient-related effects. The component distinction prevents an apparent numerical comparison from becoming misleading. A nominal static-field strength identifies one feature of a scanner; it is not the RF absorbed-energy quantity or a description of a switched gradient. Interpreting a report requires the original component and units rather than a generic description of scanner radiation.

modules.title: Static does not mean the whole scan is static

modules.label: Everyday exposure

paragraphs.text: A patient undergoes a selected examination, while staff may move repeatedly near the system or assist patients during particular tasks. The occupational communication highlights inhomogeneous fields and varied exposure during assistance and procedures. Its discussion should not be transferred into an estimate of the effects of a particular patient scan. A staff study may investigate repeated movement or assistance around a scanner, while a patient question concerns a selected examination. The observation period, activity and body position should remain attached to the finding. Removing those details could make a useful occupational report appear to answer an individual medical-exposure question that it did not test.

modules.title: Patients and staff have different patterns

modules.label: Mechanisms

paragraphs.text: ICNIRP discusses transient sensory effects associated with strong static fields and movement through them. The overall MRI environment also includes forces on susceptible objects and questions involving medical devices. These are different from a claim of long-term cancer or reproductive harm, and the absence of ionization does not remove the need for an MRI-specific safety process. The relevance of a finding depends on which interaction was actually investigated. A movement-related sensation is different from an RF-heating outcome or a response of an implanted device. Grouping them under one harm label would make it harder to understand the assessment required and would add no evidence about chronic disease.

modules.title: Several established interactions need attention

modules.label: Levels and limits

paragraphs.text: ICNIRP separates patient medical exposure from general exposure limits and discusses workers and movement separately. HSE similarly distinguishes direct health, sensory and indirect effects in its UK workplace framework. A public exposure threshold should not be treated as a stand-alone rule for whether a clinically indicated scan is appropriate. An examination involves a medical context rather than an ordinary environmental source comparison. The official source’s distinction helps explain the scope of its guidance, with no basis here for turning a worker limit or a public reference value into an individual instruction about a scan. That would require patient- and device-specific information outside this overview.

modules.title: Know whose exposure the guidance covers

modules.label: Distance

paragraphs.text: For workers, the path and speed of movement through the static field can affect transient sensations; field strength at one point is not the complete description. A site’s layout and procedures therefore matter more than a generic rule based only on distance from the scanner. Object and implanted-device issues also need their own assessment. A map and a movement record would answer complementary questions: what field exists at each position, and how a person traverses it during a task. A distance label alone supplies neither a complete route nor an operating history. That is why the source’s movement discussion should be preserved when interpreting worker observations.

modules.title: Movement and field gradients matter

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The selected communication describes sparse long-term static-field evidence and refers to earlier worker symptom reports. Those cited studies have not been converted into new independently verified cases here. A complete review would recover the original reports, separate scanner components, distinguish patients from workers and evaluate exposure history and follow-up. Scientific review remains pending; narrative context does not close that gap. Recovering the cited papers would also permit report-family and outcome checks. A position paper can mention several findings without each representing a new independent worker population. The current gap concerns those original comparisons and their methodological assessment; it should not be broadened into an unsupported claim that every possible MRI outcome lacks research.

MRI is also a clear example of why a source page and an outcome page serve different purposes. Describing scanner components can explain what a staff member or patient encounters. It cannot by itself establish whether a particular pregnancy, cognitive or cancer outcome changed. The occupational communication cites earlier symptom and long-term studies, but those citations remain leads until the original populations and results are checked. A future evidence table should therefore state which component was assessed, how exposure was determined, who was observed and what endpoint was recorded, rather than attach one health label to MRI as a whole.

modules.title: Keep the evidence gap narrow and visible

overview.text: MRI uses a combination of static magnetic fields, switched low-frequency fields and radiofrequency energy. ICNIRP’s application summary treats these components separately. Describing the system only as “non-ionizing” is correct but incomplete: each component, and the presence of metallic or electronic devices, raises a different physical question.

The recovered occupational communication discusses complex MRI exposure and transient symptoms reported in earlier worker literature. It is background synthesis, not a newly recruited MRI cohort. We have not recovered the relevant MRI-specific primary full texts for a complete long-term outcome appraisal, and that gap remains part of this page.

takeaway: MRI cannot be represented by one field number. The selected official sources explain established effects and safety scopes; direct long-term MRI-specific primary coverage remains incomplete.
title: MRI and static magnetic fields

faqs.a: No. Use the glioma-specific analysis, its diagnosis definitions and uncertainty.
faqs.q: Is a result for all brain tumours necessarily a glioma result?

faqs.a: No. Cohorts study particular histories and follow-up; new use patterns and very long latency require continued observation.
faqs.q: Does this evidence prove that every future phone technology is covered?

intro: Glioma is a specific brain-tumour outcome. Phone histories, workplace RF estimates and animal tumours answer different parts of the question.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: Registry-linked cohorts can identify incident diagnoses after baseline exposure questions, whereas case-control studies ask about previous use after diagnosis. The updated Million Women Study also considered subtype and location, but detailed tumour laterality was incomplete. A result for all brain tumours should not automatically be quoted as the result for every glioma subtype. This makes the outcome definition part of judging consistency. An analysis combining diagnoses may have more observations but answer a broader question, while a subtype analysis can be more specific and less precise. The report’s actual case definitions and available event information need to accompany either result.

modules.title: Diagnosis, subtype and latency

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The selected COSMOS summary and the full-text Million Women update do not show a clear increase in glioma with their phone-use measures. INTERPHONE’s highest recalled-use result needs the same attention as its overall pattern and limitations. In occupational INTEROCC data, results were not consistent across exposure-assignment methods or time windows. These contrasts deserve comparison rather than a vote by publication. Prospective exposure reporting, recalled histories and group-level occupational assignments have different limitations. A selected positive category needs its own precision and context retained, while an overall null pattern should not be broadened into an assertion that every exposure history and subtype was equally well studied.

There is a further difference between total calling and the dose-relevant part of that history. A handset used near the head, hands-free use and changing network conditions may have different implications even where reported call time is similar. The Million Women authors identify coarse exposure information as a limitation, while INTEROCC discusses uncertainty in group-level occupational assignments. Improved measurement would help assess whether apparently different studies examined comparable exposures. It would not justify recasting a rare positive subgroup as an established causal effect without checking prespecification, precision and the full pattern of results.

modules.title: Read cohorts and case-control results together

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: A self-reported call history is not a direct measurement of absorbed brain dose. Case-control reporting can differ after a diagnosis, while cohort use categories can misclassify changing behaviour. Job-exposure matrices average across workers whose tasks vary. Selection and multiple comparisons can also influence isolated positive results; these limitations must be assessed, rather than used automatically to dismiss or validate a finding. Longer follow-up can improve observation of later diagnoses while leaving the initial exposure variable coarse. More detailed retrospective questioning can improve some history information while introducing other reporting concerns. Appraisal has to assess those tradeoffs in the particular report, instead of assuming that one design label settles the causal question.

modules.title: Why exposure estimates can disagree

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: Long-latency cancer incidence is not established by a brief sham-controlled human RF experiment. Animal bioassays can examine tumour development under controlled exposure, but their species, whole-body dose and survival conditions differ from ordinary human calling. The NTP and Ramazzini reports belong in a separate hazard and translation assessment, not as extra human glioma cases. The contrast being controlled is therefore important: the animal work can better define exposure and ascertain pathology within the experiment, but supplies no additional phone-user follow-up. Evidence streams can inform one another without their participants, tumour sites or exposure quantities being merged into a single human risk calculation.

modules.title: Experiments provide a different kind of evidence

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: NCI separates cancer sites and exposure settings, and ICNIRP’s RF explanation addresses established adverse heating and the quantities used in exposure assessment. These serve different purposes from a glioma-specific epidemiological review. Neither the word “non-ionizing” nor a guideline comparison alone is a complete account of the observational tumour evidence. The useful role of guidance is to clarify what quantity or established interaction a technical assessment addresses. The epidemiological question still requires case ascertainment, an exposure history, suitable comparison groups and consideration of alternative explanations. An explanation of radiation physics is background to that assessment, with no substitute for the disease-specific evidence.

modules.title: Interpret classifications within their remit

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: Moving a handset away during a call can change exposure, but the selected material does not show that a headset or other accessory prevents glioma. FOPH presents hands-free options as exposure-reduction choices and cautions about shielding products that affect the connection. A reduction in a physical quantity should not be advertised as a measured reduction in cancer incidence. For a prevention study, both the exposure change and the clinical outcome would need assessment over a relevant period. A user may choose a different calling arrangement, but that choice should not be presented as a tested tumour-prevention programme when the source reports only how exposure can change.

modules.title: Exposure changes are not proven prevention

overview.text: A glioma analysis should identify how tumours were diagnosed, which subtypes were included and when exposure occurred relative to diagnosis. It should also distinguish a phone against the head from occupational RF or low-frequency exposure. Combining these as a single EMF variable obscures both biology and study design.

The source selection includes established phone studies and a recovered occupational job-exposure-matrix analysis. These are not one uniform experiment, and reports from the same cohort or research consortium must not be counted repeatedly as independent confirmation. The present synthesis is an editorial draft with scientific appraisal still pending.

takeaway: The selected prospective phone cohorts do not show increased glioma risk under their studied conditions. Case-control signals and exposure uncertainty still require careful appraisal.
title: Glioma and electromagnetic fields

faqs.a: No. They are distinct outcomes, and each needs its own estimates and limitations.
faqs.q: Can an acoustic-neuroma finding be applied to meningioma?

faqs.a: Related reports can analyse the same people or controls. Repeated publication is not equivalent to independent replication.
faqs.q: Why mention overlap if several papers agree?

intro: Meningioma should be assessed separately from glioma and acoustic neuroma. Slow development and exposure measurement shape the interpretation.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: A study may identify meningiomas through histopathology or registry linkage, with different eligibility and timing. The Swedish phone report studied diagnoses in a specified period and examined latency and cumulative use. A cumulative calling category records recalled behaviour; it does not directly measure energy deposited in the tissue where a tumour develops. A history may describe when use began, how much calling accumulated or which technology was used. Each variable asks a slightly different exposure question and can have different reporting error. The measurement description needs to stay attached to the result rather than all such categories being summarised as one directly observed brain dose.

modules.title: Define cases and the exposure window

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The Swedish phone study found no conclusive association; a highest cumulative-use signal was not accompanied by a significant increasing latency pattern. Million Women reported no increased incidence in its phone-use categories. The occupational ELF report found no overall association, and INTEROCC RF results were not consistent across methods and windows. Those are bounded findings, not a proof covering every exposure history. An isolated highest-category signal and the absence of a consistent latency pattern are both part of the Swedish result. Retaining them together is more informative than selecting either as the paper’s entire conclusion. Occupational matrices and prospective phone categories then need their own assessment before apparent agreement is treated as evidence of the same causal contrast.

Latency is especially easy to oversimplify. Years since first use, years of cumulative use and time windows before diagnosis describe different features of an exposure history. The Swedish phone paper examined several of these and did not find a consistently increasing latency pattern. The occupational reports used their own timing and exposure definitions. A synthesis needs to compare those definitions and the numbers informing each category, rather than treating every “long-term” result as identical. A review should also retain the possibility of exposure misclassification in the cohorts and matrices when interpreting the absence of a coherent pattern.

modules.title: Look for a coherent pattern

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: The Swedish phone analysis had few truly unexposed people and considerable use of multiple technologies. The occupational ELF matrix assigned group values without individual measurements. INTEROCC additionally discusses reporting, selection and multiple comparisons. These issues affect how much weight to place on both an isolated elevation and an overall null pattern; a formal appraisal needs explicit judgments. Longer follow-up alone cannot remove those exposure and selection problems. The reference group also matters: comparing heavier users with people who have little use is not identical to comparing exposed people with a truly unexposed population. Where technologies are used together, attribution to one source needs additional care. Those features help define what a reported contrast actually estimates.

modules.title: Measurement can conceal or create patterns

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: A brief controlled human exposure study can test an immediate physiological effect, but cannot directly determine later meningioma incidence. The relevant long-term studies here are observational. Controlled animal experiments address hazard under their own conditions, and translating them would require matching tumour biology and tissue dose rather than treating all tumours as interchangeable. This also limits what a negative short-term test can rule out. A laboratory task may be measured precisely while never observing the long-term diagnosis being discussed. The experiment can answer its immediate question well and still leave meningioma incidence to a different type of study.

modules.title: Short experiments cannot observe long latency

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: NCI’s overview distinguishes cancer outcomes and exposure settings rather than offering one personal-risk figure for EMFs. RF and low-frequency guidance also address different interactions and quantities. These explanations help frame exposure, but do not replace a meningioma-specific assessment of latency, case ascertainment, exposure error and study overlap. The distinction between RF and ELF is especially important because this page includes both occupational streams. Similar-looking exposure categories can represent different quantities and assignment methods. A source-specific comparison first identifies the field and its measurement or proxy before considering whether the meningioma results support a coherent pattern.

modules.title: Keep broad agency context in proportion

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected sources do not establish an EMF avoidance programme or product that prevents or treats meningioma. An exposure-reduction option may alter a handset or workplace configuration, but proving a health benefit needs an appropriate outcome comparison. The website’s role is to distinguish those claims while the scientific review remains pending. A workplace assessment may still be appropriate for its defined technical purpose, and a hands-free arrangement can change phone exposure. Those are useful facts without a demonstrated effect on meningioma incidence. Treating an exposure-management measure as prevention would add a clinical conclusion that the cited material does not establish.

modules.title: Do not convert an exposure option into treatment

overview.text: Meningioma is a distinct tumour diagnosis, not a synonym for all brain cancer. The selected studies use specific case definitions and exposure histories. Some analyse phone use, others occupational RF or ELF estimates; a result in one of these settings should not become a verdict about the others.

Recovery adds the Swedish phone report, the Swedish occupational ELF analysis and INTEROCC’s RF analysis alongside the prospective Million Women update. The Swedish reports and INTEROCC each belong to broader research families. Independent-family reconciliation and scientific appraisal remain unfinished, even though their source-specific findings can be explained.

takeaway: The recovered phone and occupational analyses do not show a consistent meningioma association. Their limitations and overlapping study families remain important.
title: Meningioma and electromagnetic fields

faqs.a: No. Tinnitus is a symptom; acoustic neuroma is a diagnosed tumour. They must not be merged in an evidence count.
faqs.q: Is tinnitus the same outcome as acoustic neuroma?

faqs.a: Tumour-related hearing changes can alter the ear used, and retrospective recall can also differ after diagnosis. These effects can bias laterality analyses.
faqs.q: Why are same-side findings difficult?

intro: Also called vestibular schwannoma, this is a rare outcome for which hearing symptoms, side of phone use and long latency complicate the research.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The relevant outcome is a tumour diagnosis, while side of phone use is usually recalled. Hearing loss can change which ear someone uses even before diagnosis, and awareness of a tumour can affect later recall. The five-country report explicitly discusses these potentially opposing biases. Neither the usual ear nor handedness is a direct absorbed-dose measurement. The resulting error need not point in one direction. A person might change their preferred ear because hearing has changed, and a later account may be influenced by knowing the tumour side. An apparent same-side pattern therefore needs those competing explanations assessed alongside the exposure hypothesis.

modules.title: Diagnosis and side of use are separate variables

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The five-country analysis found no overall raised risk with regular use or in the first decade, with an uncertain long-use same-side signal. The pooled Swedish analysis reported higher odds with wireless-phone use and longer latency. Million Women did not find an increased acoustic-neuroma incidence in its reported phone-use categories. These patterns require comparison of design and exposure histories, rather than a simple paper vote. The longer-use signals remain part of the evidence, with no reason to omit them because they are difficult to interpret. Their meaning depends on how use, side, latency and comparison groups were defined. Equally, the cohort’s lack of an observed increase retains its own population, exposure and rare-outcome precision limits.

The cohort and case-control designs also place exposure reporting at different points in time. Million Women collected use information before registry follow-up, reducing the opportunity for a diagnosis to change the baseline answer. Its limitation was comparatively simple use information in an older female population. The acoustic-neuroma case-control papers obtained more detailed histories but faced retrospective reporting and participation issues. These trade-offs are reasons to examine the studies together, not reasons to assume one design is error-free. Longer follow-up and better characterised exposure would be useful, particularly where the outcome is uncommon and the longest-use groups remain small.

modules.title: The selected results do not all agree

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Long-use categories can contain few cases, making estimates imprecise and sensitive to categorisation. Control participation and recalled call duration also matter in case-control work. The Swedish authors pooled their newer period with earlier data because the newer acoustic-neuroma sample was small; that pooling expands information without creating a new independent replication of the earlier study. Pooling can improve the amount of information for an uncommon outcome while preserving the biases of the component studies. A later pooled paper and its earlier reports should therefore be linked as one research family where they reuse participants. Publication dates alone do not establish independent confirmation.

modules.title: Rare outcomes make estimates fragile

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: A sham-controlled short-term RF study cannot directly observe a tumour with long development. Animal schwannoma findings can raise hazard questions, but a rat heart schwannoma is not an additional human vestibular schwannoma. Translation requires attention to tissue, species, dose and exposure timing, with human incidence remaining a separate evidential track. A shared tumour-cell label does not remove the difference between tissues and exposure systems. The animal study can raise a biological question for human research, but the translation must be argued using the actual conditions. It cannot be accomplished by adding the animal lesions to the human diagnosis count.

modules.title: What experimental evidence could establish

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: NCI separates different cancer sites and exposure settings, while ICNIRP explains RF quantities and established heating effects. These sources help prevent a room-field reading or a general RF label from being mistaken for a tumour-risk estimate. They do not erase the need to evaluate long-use histories and rare-outcome precision in each acoustic-neuroma study. A useful account consequently reads technical and disease evidence together without giving them the same function. The exposure document helps interpret quantities and interactions; the tumour studies address incidence under their own histories. Neither a general agency statement nor one selected epidemiological category completes that combined appraisal.

modules.title: Agency context is broader than this diagnosis

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: FOPH describes hands-free arrangements as ways to reduce head exposure during calls. The selected material does not demonstrate that a particular headset, shield or reduced-calling programme prevents acoustic neuroma. Nor can symptoms alone identify an RF cause. A prevention claim would require suitable comparative outcomes, not merely a change in the physical exposure. A change in symptoms or calling habits would not, by itself, demonstrate prevention of a slowly developing tumour. The endpoint and observation period would have to match the claim. Keeping that requirement clear avoids presenting an exposure-reduction option or a consumer accessory as an established clinical intervention.

modules.title: Exposure reduction has a narrower claim

overview.text: An acoustic-neuroma analysis needs to distinguish a confirmed diagnosis from self-reported tinnitus or hearing difficulty. Those symptoms may be relevant to detection or behaviour, but they are not tumour diagnoses. Our sources include a five-country INTERPHONE analysis, a pooled Swedish case-control report and the prospective Million Women update.

The long-latency question deserves a direct account of both signals and limitations. Some reports reuse earlier populations, so a list of publications overstates the number of independent study families unless overlap is reconciled. That reconciliation and a complete scientific appraisal remain pending.

takeaway: Selected studies differ: some case-control analyses report long-use signals, while prospective data do not show an increase. Laterality results are particularly vulnerable to interpretation problems.

faqs.a: Not unless a diagnosis is confirmed. The cited study kept that suspected group separate from confirmed breast cancers.
faqs.q: Are women referred for mammography cancer cases?

faqs.a: No. Each diagnosis, population and exposure needs its own evidence and uncertainty.
faqs.q: Does one negative cancer-site analysis settle all cancer questions?

intro: “Other cancers” is a directory of distinct research questions, not one outcome. Breast, eye and other tumour sites require separate comparisons.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The breast-cancer report distinguishes histologically confirmed cases, an exploratory group referred for mammography without a diagnosis, and controls. Suspected cases must not be counted as confirmed cancers. The Million Women eye analysis, by contrast, concerns incident tumours recorded during follow-up. These case definitions and timings should remain visible in any comparison. This prevents an exploratory referral group from inflating the disease denominator. It also explains why a cross-sectional comparison of clinical groups and a prospective incident-case analysis require separate rows. They answer different site-specific questions even when both papers collect some information about mobile-phone use.

The exposure hypothesis should also identify which tissue is expected to receive the relevant energy. Phone-call duration can be useful as a behavioural measure while saying little about whether a device was near the chest, used hands-free or carried elsewhere between calls. The breast-cancer report includes phone placement questions, but its retrospective design does not turn those answers into measured tissue dose. In the eye-tumour cohort analysis, the number of events and the use categories set another limit on interpretation. Keeping site, dose proxy and study design together prevents a broad headline from outgrowing the data.

modules.title: Start with a confirmed diagnosis

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The breast-cancer authors report a calling-time association, but the printed group totals conflict with the Methods and screen-time reference coding conflicts with broad prose claims. Its numerical effects remain held pending clarification. The cohort did not find increased eye-tumour risk in its reported phone-use groups. These are different outcomes and populations; one cannot cancel or confirm the other as a generic test of cancer. A printed inconsistency is a reason to withhold the dependent estimate until the source is clarified, rather than to choose whichever total gives the preferred interpretation. The qualitative report can still be described with that limitation. The eye-tumour result should likewise retain its own event information and exposure definitions.

modules.title: Describe the actual selected observations

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Daily calling and screen time can correlate with sleep, light exposure, socioeconomic factors and other behaviour. In the breast study they do not isolate absorbed RF dose in breast tissue. Retrospective reporting and control selection are additional concerns. A prospective design reduces some recall problems, but coarse exposure categories and small numbers of uncommon diagnoses can still limit a cohort analysis. The clinical question is exposure specific: which energy, at which tissue and during what relevant history? Device habits can accompany many other activities. Adjustment and careful timing may address parts of that problem, with no guarantee that a behavioural questionnaire separates every causal pathway associated with the habit.

modules.title: Behaviour is not the same as tissue dose

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: An animal cancer experiment can investigate a hazard under controlled conditions; a cell experiment can examine a pathway. Neither directly measures human breast or eye cancer incidence. The NTP and Ramazzini findings therefore need their own exposure and translation assessment. Adding every animal or cellular result to the same human cancer count would misrepresent the independent evidence. The source of apparent replication must also be checked. Multiple assays from the same experiment or several papers from a shared animal programme add information about different endpoints without automatically creating independent evidence. Human cancer risk still requires a transparent translation argument and disease-specific observational comparisons.

modules.title: Keep experimental endpoints separate

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: NCI provides context on sources, cancer research and exposure measurement. Its distinction between job-title proxies, measured fields and household sources is particularly important here. The current page uses that framework without assigning a new certainty grade or claiming that one agency summary completes a review of every organ, occupation and frequency range. The strongest useful scope here is therefore the named organ and exposure setting. An incomplete breast-cancer comparison cannot be filled by an unrelated eye-tumour result, and a general source description cannot supply the missing clinical data. Wider coverage requires additional site-specific sources and their original methods.

modules.title: A broad overview is a map, not a verdict

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected studies do not test whether a phone accessory or household shielding programme prevents these cancers. FOPH’s mobile-phone document distinguishes exposure-reduction options from health outcomes and notes that shielding can affect the connection. A genuine prevention claim needs an outcome-specific comparison over a suitable period, with other behavioural changes considered. Even a demonstrated reduction in a particular field quantity would leave the proposed cancer benefit to be tested. A comparison changing several habits at once would also need to establish which change was responsible. The current sources support separating those questions, with no basis for an accessory-based prevention claim.

modules.title: No general cancer-prevention product is established

overview.text: Cancer sites differ in biology, diagnosis and relevant exposure. NCI’s overview separates household low-frequency fields, wireless RF and occupational settings. A claim about all cancers should not be assembled by combining unrelated outcomes, exposure sources and study designs into a single positive-or-negative total.

The current recovered selection adds a multicentre breast-cancer case-control report and a cohort’s eye-tumour analysis. These are selected leads, not an exhaustive review of every cancer site. Breast-cancer findings need scientific appraisal, and a wider site-specific source search and family reconciliation remain unfinished.

takeaway: The selected breast-cancer report has unresolved group-count and interpretation problems, so its numerical effects are held. The separate eye-tumour cohort analysis does not establish a general cancer effect of EMFs.

faqs.a: No. Call frequency can correlate with stress and behaviour, and it is an imperfect measure of absorbed RF exposure.
faqs.q: Does an association with phone calls identify RF as the cause?

faqs.a: Its city and sample counts overlap the fuller Babol report, while date descriptions differ. The relationship remains unresolved and it is not counted as independent confirmation.
faqs.q: Can the infertility letter be counted as another independent study?

intro: Infertility, miscarriage, preterm birth and fetal growth are different outcomes. Exposure proxies and timing are central to each comparison.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The Babol study compared clinic-defined infertility with controls, using residential proximity to power lines. The two-town pregnancy cohort followed miscarriage while recording fields at outdoor locations. The birth-cohort analysis studied gestational duration, fetal growth and birth weight, and the induction study used reported delivery information. These outcomes require different denominators and observation windows.

modules.title: Outcome definitions and timing matter

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: Babol reported an infertility association with proximity. The miscarriage cohort differed by field metric: front-door averages were not predictive, while maximum alley values were associated. More frequent maternal calling was associated with shorter gestation in a four-cohort analysis, without a fetal-growth or birth-weight association. Some induction-use categories related weakly to preterm delivery, but the authors judged bias and other explanations important.

The four-cohort pregnancy paper is another example of complementary information within established study families. It combines cohort-specific estimates rather than recruiting four new independent replications of every earlier birth-cohort report. The authors note that reported calling could reflect factors such as stress and that some information was collected well after pregnancy. The induction study has a different exposure proxy and its own follow-up and response problems. A reliable overview needs those differences beside the findings; it should not convert the presence of several papers into a single combined estimate of risk from any electrical device.

A retrospective Konya hospital study reported higher listed phone-model SAR among mothers of babies classified as small for gestational age, while recalled daily use-time was similar between growth groups. It assigned SAR from a phone listing rather than measuring maternal or fetal dose. Selection, recall, no reported adjusted causal model and a covariate-table inconsistency limit interpretation. The same-data prediction cutoff is not an independently validated safety threshold.

modules.title: The recovered findings are not one pattern

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Distance is not a personal field measurement. Outdoor readings without activity records do not describe every pregnancy’s dose. Phone-call frequency can reflect stress and other behaviours, and retrospective reporting adds uncertainty. Induction use and medical outcomes were self-reported in an internet panel. These issues affect causal interpretation even when a statistical association is present.

modules.title: Exposure and confounding remain major limits

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The induction-cooker measurement study helps estimate fields from cooking position and appliance features, but does not show a pregnancy effect. Its fixed-position estimates also require duration information and wider validation. Animal or isolated-cell results would answer separate mechanistic questions and cannot be substituted for human conception or birth outcomes without a justified translation.

modules.title: A measurement model is not an outcome trial

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: FOPH’s induction fact sheet distinguishes measured configurations and limit comparisons from the limited pregnancy literature. HSE’s workplace framework separately considers expectant workers at particular risk, within its UK remit. Neither document makes all home sources equivalent or supplies an individual prediction from one household reading. Formal source appraisal remains necessary for each outcome.

The recovered RF reproductive protocol includes pregnancy and developmental outcomes in experimental mammals exposed in utero. That experimental stream is distinct from observational pregnancy studies in people. Its planned exposure controls and bias assessment describe how evidence would be assessed, rather than a completed conclusion about miscarriage, birth outcomes or human risk.

modules.title: Guidance and clinical outcomes have different scopes

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: These selected reports do not test an EMF product, avoidance programme or household distance rule as a way to improve conception or birth outcomes. Changing a source can alter a physical exposure while leaving the causal and clinical questions unresolved. A useful future study would measure exposure more directly, define outcomes prospectively and account for stress, socioeconomic circumstances and other environmental contributors.

modules.title: No reproductive treatment has been demonstrated

overview.text: This page separates the ability to conceive from outcomes after conception, including miscarriage, gestational duration and birth weight. It also separates phone calling, power-line proximity, residential magnetic-field readings and induction cooking. Those measures do not represent one common dose, even when reports are grouped under “EMF.”

The recovered full texts provide specific observations, with scientific review still pending. Repeated reports from the same clinic or cohort are not automatically independent confirmation. This remains selected-source coverage rather than a completed reproductive systematic review, and the present selection does not resolve every source or pregnancy outcome.

takeaway: The recovered observational reports are mixed and use imperfect exposure measures. They do not establish a general reproductive effect or a proven EMF intervention.
title: Female fertility, pregnancy and EMFs

faqs.a: No. Its size, duration, location, cause and clinical consequences matter; physiological variation is not automatically harm.
faqs.q: Does any temperature change mean injury?

faqs.a: No. It concerns a short, controlled low-field experiment and superficial skin outcomes in healthy adults.
faqs.q: Does the 26 GHz result prove every RF exposure is non-thermal?

intro: Heating is a physical interaction with a dose, time and tissue context. A measured temperature change and a harmful thermal injury are different endpoints.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: Skin temperature, core temperature, local tissue absorption, perceived warmth and a diagnosed burn are not interchangeable. A superficial infrared image may detect one pattern while saying little about another tissue. The 26 GHz experiment explicitly limits its conclusions to monitored skin measures in healthy young adults under controlled conditions, rather than validating every guideline threshold. The relevant negative finding is bounded by that instrument, location and observation window. It can show that a particular protocol did not detect a consistent superficial response while leaving a separate question about another tissue or duration unanswered. Reporting those limits makes the result more precise rather than less useful.

Measurement resolution also defines what a negative thermal finding means. The 26 GHz authors discuss their sample, monitoring interval and restriction to superficial sites as limitations. Their conclusion is about changes detectable with that protocol, rather than an assertion that every tissue was continuously measured or that arbitrarily small differences were excluded. In workplace reports, perceived warmth and a medical examination are different observations again. A table should identify the instrument or ascertainment method and exposure duration alongside the endpoint. That information lets the reader distinguish a physical measurement, a subjective sensation and a clinically significant injury.

modules.title: Choose a thermal endpoint before interpreting it

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The acute 26 GHz study did not detect a consistent skin-temperature response at its tested low fields; temperatures also changed over time during sham sessions. A pooled regional-analysis label differs between prose and Table 1, so every analysis cannot simply be called null. At the other end of the exposure spectrum, the occupational review describes suspected overexposure and repair accidents. These are useful observations within their respective conditions, not contradictory results that can be averaged into one heating score. The sham changes are informative because they show why temperature drift over a session should not automatically be assigned to the RF source. Accident reports then describe a different exposure regime and endpoint. The comparison needs to preserve those operating conditions before trying to reconcile the observations.

modules.title: The dose and scenario determine applicability

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Ambient conditions, movement, clothing and normal thermoregulation can change measured temperatures. The controlled study used matched exposure and sham sessions to distinguish an RF-related effect from changes over time. In everyday settings, warmth from an electronic product’s battery or surface is also a different pathway from RF absorbed in tissue; the exposure method must isolate what is being tested. A change during exposure is therefore only the start of the analysis. The appropriate contrast asks whether it differs from the matched sham pattern, while considering the monitoring method and normal variation. Feeling warmth near an operating device does not by itself identify the pathway that produced the sensation.

modules.title: Temperature has many ordinary influences

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The experiment used a blinded randomized crossover design with infrared monitoring during brief genuine and sham sessions. That strengthens the specific comparison, but its small healthy-adult sample, acute duration and superficial measures limit transfer to children, impaired thermoregulation or prolonged exposure. A null result under those conditions is narrower than proof that RF cannot produce heating. The crossover comparison uses each person across conditions, which is different from adding each session as a new participant. Its strength is control of a narrowly defined exposure contrast. The source’s reporting issue and the limits of its endpoints remain relevant even where the experimental allocation is stronger than an observational survey.

modules.title: What the controlled study can establish

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: ICNIRP distinguishes external reference levels from basic restrictions on absorbed quantities and uses frequency-, body-region- and duration-specific assessment. FDA’s oven explanation gives a practical example: microwave energy deliberately heats food inside an enclosure, while outside leakage and thermal burns require separate consideration. A product’s cooking output cannot be substituted for a person’s absorbed dose. The same distinction applies when interpreting a device’s output specification. The energy intended for a cavity or another technical task is not automatically the quantity absorbed by a nearby person. Assessment must follow the actual source-to-body conditions before the appropriate restriction or reference level can be interpreted.

modules.title: Limits use specific quantities and averaging

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: Workplace controls address defined equipment, tasks and established hazards, including maintenance situations that can bypass normal safeguards. That purpose should not be confused with evidence that lowering an already low environmental reading improves sleep, fertility or cancer outcomes. Such benefits require their own comparative studies; the selected thermal sources do not demonstrate them. Evidence that a control reduces an established exposure hazard is not evidence that every further reduction produces a clinical benefit. A study of sleep or fertility would need those outcomes observed with an appropriate comparator. The thermal material identifies its own physical and occupational questions rather than answering unrelated health hypotheses.

modules.title: Preventing overexposure is different from proving a chronic benefit

overview.text: RF energy absorbed in tissue can become heat, and ICNIRP’s explanation ties established adverse heating to dose, duration and the body region involved. This differs from the low-frequency framework of induced electric fields and stimulation. A generic meter reading cannot identify either an internal temperature change or an injury.

The recovered controlled experiment measured superficial skin temperature during a defined 26 GHz exposure and sham condition. A separate thermal-mechanism report carries an unresolved correction signal and is held from this page’s findings. Occupational accidents and ordinary environmental exposures are presented as distinct scenarios. Scientific review is pending.

takeaway: RF can heat tissue at sufficient exposure. The recovered acute 26 GHz experiment found no consistent skin-temperature response under its tested conditions. A pooled-analysis discrepancy remains unresolved, and this does not settle every thermal scenario.

faqs.q: Does an association with EHS prove that fields caused tinnitus?

faqs.a: No. It concerns the call-time measures, population and follow-up studied, not every RF source or all aspects of device use.
faqs.q: Is a call-time null result proof about every device and sound exposure?

intro: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a field measurement or a tumour diagnosis. Phone use, perceived sensitivity and acoustic exposure need separate consideration.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The Regensburg study assessed tinnitus occurrence and severity using questionnaires; COSMOS also relied on later self-reported hearing symptoms. Self-report is relevant to the symptom experience, but can miss differences in onset, persistence or severity. A tinnitus questionnaire is not a diagnosis of acoustic neuroma and should not be counted as a brain-tumour outcome. An analysis of new onset also differs from a comparison of prevalent symptoms at one survey. The time sequence and symptom definition determine which claim the data can address. Keeping those details visible prevents a questionnaire association being recast as a confirmed diagnosis or a specific RF-induced injury.

modules.title: Record occurrence, timing and severity

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The COSMOS authors described no clear tinnitus gradient with baseline call time. The smaller EHS comparison found tinnitus more common in the self-described EHS group, while its phone-use measures did not show a tinnitus relationship. Its proposed shared vulnerability mechanism was a hypothesis rather than an established causal explanation. Exact COSMOS tinnitus counts and estimates remain held because the printed text and tables do not fully agree. That source issue prevents a stronger numerical interpretation; it does not establish the EHS paper’s proposed mechanism or convert a symptom association into evidence of measured RF causation.

The timing in COSMOS is useful because recorded calls preceded the follow-up symptoms, but the record covered a limited baseline period. It was not continuous tracking of every participant’s later phone use. The smaller EHS study’s matched surroundings were intended as rough exposure proxies, not a direct dosimetry programme. Their null phone-use results and their different positive or negative symptom associations should therefore remain tied to the measured variables. A broader review would need to examine hearing-related factors, symptom definitions and changes in device use without assuming that a symptom report identifies the energy source responsible.

modules.title: What the selected studies found

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Call time does not perfectly represent absorbed RF, especially across networks and hands-free use. It also fails to describe every sound or behavioural exposure associated with a device. COSMOS used a short baseline record and symptoms at later follow-up, while the EHS study used rough environmental matching and self-report. These limitations constrain inference about a particular causal agent. The source record should therefore say which alternative was actually measured. A call log can improve the timing of a behavioural exposure while still leaving sound dose and later use poorly observed. A sensitivity label can describe a participant group without identifying the physical agent responsible for each symptom.

modules.title: Phone behaviour is a bundle of exposures

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The recovered tinnitus papers do not provide a blinded intervention showing that a specified RF exposure triggers tinnitus. Prospective follow-up improves the timing of exposure measurement relative to outcome but remains observational. The cross-sectional EHS comparison cannot establish which condition came first, so its correlation should not become a direct exposure challenge result. Those designs can identify patterns worth testing, while leaving the direct trigger question open. A controlled challenge would require a specified source, genuine masking, relevant symptom ascertainment and an observation window suited to the hypothesis. None of those design features can be supplied by relabelling an observational correlation.

modules.title: Blinding and follow-up answer different questions

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: WHO’s historical EHS fact sheet recognizes that symptoms can be real and disabling while distinguishing symptom experience from attribution to EMF. It is not a current tinnitus-specific review or a diagnostic test for a person’s symptoms. That distinction supports careful investigation without treating a reported sensitivity label as a measured exposure mechanism. Recognising the symptom burden and evaluating an attribution are compatible tasks. The historical document helps explain that distinction, with no authority here to diagnose a person or establish the cause of their tinnitus. A current outcome-specific appraisal still needs the actual symptom and exposure studies.

modules.title: Take symptoms seriously while testing attribution

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected evidence does not show that an EMF shield, avoidance programme or phone accessory treats tinnitus. A change in device use can also change sound, sleep routines, stress and expectations. A credible intervention study would compare a defined treatment, specify relevant outcomes and account for those factors rather than infer an RF effect from improvement after several changes at once. The comparison should also distinguish an improvement after a change from an improvement attributable to a particular field reduction. Without that separation, the study may support a broader intervention while leaving its proposed RF mechanism unresolved. The selected reports do not supply such a treatment trial.

modules.title: Improvement does not isolate the active change

overview.text: A tinnitus study should specify what participants were asked, whether symptoms were already present and when exposure information was collected. Operator-recorded call time, subjective electromagnetic sensitivity and a measured RF dose are different variables. They cannot be substituted for each other just because all appear in a discussion of phones.

The two recovered reports illustrate that distinction. COSMOS related baseline calling records to later symptoms, while the Regensburg comparison studied people reporting EHS and matched controls at one time. Their populations and designs differ, and related cohort reports do not represent new independent participants. Scientific review remains pending.

takeaway: The recovered COSMOS follow-up found no call-time association with tinnitus. A smaller cross-sectional study linked tinnitus with reported EHS, without establishing fields as the cause.
